skill_title: Describe and analyse galvanic and electrolytic cells
notes: 20 items: 10 lifted, 10 fresh. Galvanic cells (spontaneous, anode = NEG); electrolytic cells (driven, anode = POS); cell notation; electron flow; salt bridge; electroplating; refining; NaCl electrolysis.

items.question: Define ELECTROLYSIS.
items.expectedAnswer: Using electrical energy from an external source to drive a non-spontaneous redox reaction.
items.explanation: Key features: electrical energy IN, non-spontaneous reaction, external power source.
options: Producing electrical energy from a spontaneous reaction.
Breaking a substance down by heating it strongly.
Using electrical energy from an external source to drive a non-spontaneous redox reaction.

items.question: Define an ELECTROLYTIC CELL.
items.expectedAnswer: A cell that uses electrical energy (external power) to drive a non-spontaneous reaction.
items.explanation: Same idea as electrolysis: external source drives non-spontaneous redox.
options: A cell that uses electrical energy (external power) to drive a non-spontaneous reaction.
A cell that generates electricity from a spontaneous reaction.
A cell that operates with no external connections.

items.question: State the energy conversion in a GALVANIC CELL.
items.expectedAnswer: Chemical (potential) energy into electrical energy.
items.explanation: Galvanic: spontaneous redox releases energy ⇒ chemical → electrical. (Opposite of electrolytic.)
options: Electrical energy into chemical energy.
Chemical (potential) energy into electrical energy.
Heat energy into electrical energy.

items.question: State the function of the SALT BRIDGE in an electrochemical (galvanic) cell.
items.expectedAnswer: It maintains electrical neutrality by allowing ions to flow between the half-cells.
items.explanation: Key roles: (1) maintain neutrality; (2) complete circuit (ion flow, not electron flow).
options: It carries electrons between the two half-cells.
It speeds up the reaction, acting like a catalyst.
It maintains electrical neutrality by allowing ions to flow between the half-cells.

items.question: In a GALVANIC cell, which electrode is the ANODE — POSITIVE or NEGATIVE? At which electrode does oxidation occur?
items.expectedAnswer: Anode = negative; oxidation occurs at the anode.
items.explanation: Galvanic anode: NEG. Oxidation always at anode. Cathode in galvanic is POS.
options: Anode = negative; oxidation occurs at the anode.
Anode = positive; oxidation occurs at the anode.
Anode = negative; reduction occurs at the anode.

items.question: In an ELECTROLYTIC cell, the anode is connected to:
options: The positive terminal of the external battery (anode = POS)
The negative terminal of the external battery (anode = NEG)
Neither — anodes have no fixed polarity
It depends on the half-reactions
items.expectedAnswer: The positive terminal of the external battery (anode = POS)
items.explanation: Electrolytic cell anode = POSITIVE (connected to + terminal of battery). Opposite of galvanic. Oxidation still occurs at the anode (definition unchanged).

items.question: In which direction do ELECTRONS flow in the external circuit of a galvanic cell?
items.expectedAnswer: From the anode (−) to the cathode (+) through the external wire.
items.explanation: External: anode → cathode (electrons). Internal (salt bridge): ions move to maintain neutrality.
options: From the cathode to the anode through the external wire.
From the anode (−) to the cathode (+) through the external wire.
Through the salt bridge, from anode to cathode.

items.question: In the electrolysis of NaCl(aq), in which direction do ELECTRONS flow in the external circuit?
items.expectedAnswer: From the anode to the cathode through the external circuit.
items.explanation: External flow: anode → cathode in BOTH cell types. Power source drives the flow in electrolytic.
options: From the cathode to the anode in the external circuit.
Through the electrolyte solution itself.
From the anode to the cathode through the external circuit.

items.question: Write the CELL NOTATION for a galvanic cell with aluminium anode and oxygen cathode (Al → Al³⁺; O₂ → H₂O at Pt electrode).
items.expectedAnswer: Al(s) | Al³⁺(aq) || H⁺(aq), O₂(g) | Pt(s)
items.explanation: Cell notation: anode on left, cathode on right; '|' is phase boundary; '||' is salt bridge. Pt is used as an inert electrode for the gas half-cell.
options: Al(s) | Al³⁺(aq) || H⁺(aq), O₂(g) | Pt(s)
Pt(s) | O₂(g), H⁺(aq) || Al³⁺(aq) | Al(s)
Al(s) || Al³⁺(aq) | H⁺(aq) || O₂(g) | Pt(s)

items.question: In cell notation, what does a SINGLE LINE '|' represent?
items.expectedAnswer: A phase boundary (interface between two different phases).
items.explanation: '|' = phase boundary; '||' = salt bridge.
options: The salt bridge.
A phase boundary (interface between two different phases).
The external wire connection.

items.question: In the zinc electroplating of a steel spring using a Zn(NO₃)₂ electrolyte, which electrode is the ANODE: the zinc electrode or the steel spring?
items.expectedAnswer: The zinc electrode is the anode (Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻).
items.explanation: Electroplating: object to be plated = cathode; metal source = anode. The metal anode dissolves and is replated on the cathode.
options: The steel spring is the anode.
Both electrodes act as the anode.
The zinc electrode is the anode (Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻).

items.question: Write the half-reaction at the metal spring (cathode) in the electroplating cell from the previous question.
items.expectedAnswer: Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Zn (reduction — zinc deposits onto the spring).
items.explanation: Cathode: reduction. Zn²⁺ from the solution is reduced to Zn metal, plating the spring.
options: Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Zn (reduction — zinc deposits onto the spring).
Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻
2H₂O + 2e⁻ → H₂ + 2OH⁻

items.question: In the electrolysis of NaCl(aq), does the pH of the solution INCREASE, DECREASE or STAY THE SAME during electrolysis? Give a reason.
items.expectedAnswer: pH increases — water is reduced at the cathode, producing OH⁻.
items.explanation: Cathode produces OH⁻ ⇒ solution becomes basic ⇒ pH rises.
options: pH decreases — H⁺ accumulates at the cathode.
pH increases — water is reduced at the cathode, producing OH⁻.
pH stays the same — electrolysis doesn't affect pH.

items.question: Decomposing CuCl₂ → Cu + Cl₂ requires:
options: A platinum catalyst
An external power source (electrolysis)
Heat alone
Sunlight
items.expectedAnswer: An external power source (electrolysis)
items.explanation: Decomposing a stable ionic compound into its elements is non-spontaneous ⇒ requires electrolysis (electrical energy input).

items.question: Compare GALVANIC vs ELECTROLYTIC cells: state TWO key differences.
items.expectedAnswer: Galvanic = spontaneous (anode negative); electrolytic = non-spontaneous, needs external power (anode positive).
items.explanation: Spontaneity and polarity convention are the two main differences. Oxidation is always at the anode in both.
options: Galvanic = non-spontaneous; electrolytic = spontaneous.
Both are spontaneous and both have a negative anode.
Galvanic = spontaneous (anode negative); electrolytic = non-spontaneous, needs external power (anode positive).

items.question: In a Cu/Zn galvanic cell, identify the (a) anode, (b) cathode, (c) overall cell reaction. (E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V; E°(Zn²⁺/Zn) = −0.76 V.)
items.expectedAnswer: Anode: Zn (Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻); cathode: Cu (Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu); overall: Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu.
items.explanation: More negative E° = anode. Standard galvanic cell example.
options: Anode: Zn (Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻); cathode: Cu (Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu); overall: Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu.
Anode: Cu; cathode: Zn; overall: Cu + Zn²⁺ → Cu²⁺ + Zn.
Anode: Zn (positive); cathode: Cu (negative).

items.question: In the refining of copper, an impure copper anode is dissolved into solution and pure copper deposits on the cathode. What is the cell type, and which is the anode?
items.expectedAnswer: An electrolytic cell; the impure copper is the anode.
items.explanation: Refining = electrolytic. Impure source is the anode (dissolves); pure metal deposits on cathode.
options: A galvanic cell; the pure copper is the anode.
An electrolytic cell; the impure copper is the anode.
An electrolytic cell; the pure copper is the anode.

items.question: A learner says: 'Electrons flow through the salt bridge in a galvanic cell.' Is this correct?
items.expectedAnswer: Incorrect — electrons flow through the external wire; the salt bridge carries ions.
items.explanation: Common misconception. External wire: electrons. Salt bridge: ions.
options: Correct — electrons flow through the salt bridge.
Correct — both electrons and ions flow through the salt bridge.
Incorrect — electrons flow through the external wire; the salt bridge carries ions.

items.question: Why does the mass of the ANODE in a galvanic cell DECREASE over time?
items.expectedAnswer: Oxidation occurs there — metal atoms lose electrons and dissolve as ions.
items.explanation: Anode loses material to solution; cathode gains material from solution. Standard galvanic cell behaviour.
options: Oxidation occurs there — metal atoms lose electrons and dissolve as ions.
Metal ions from solution deposit onto it.
The anode evaporates because of the heat produced.

items.question: In an electrolytic cell, why doesn't the anode of an inert electrode (e.g. carbon) typically dissolve, even though oxidation occurs there?
items.expectedAnswer: An inert electrode doesn't react itself; species in the solution are oxidised instead.
items.explanation: Inert electrode: surface for reaction, doesn't oxidise. Active electrode: itself oxidises.
options: Carbon is a metal that strongly resists oxidation.
An inert electrode doesn't react itself; species in the solution are oxidised instead.
No oxidation actually occurs at an inert anode.
